Yes. The app is MIT-licensed, and the Google APIs it uses are free within their usage limits.

### Where is my data stored?

On Windows, the `%LOCALAPPDATA%\seowatcher` folder holds the database, your encrypted Google credentials and the logs; uninstalling the app leaves it in place. On Docker, everything is in the `seotracker_data` volume.

### What does the app connect to?

Google (Search Console, Analytics, PageSpeed), the site you audit, and GitHub for version checks. If you connect an AI assistant, the data the assistant reads can go to that assistant's provider; that connection is optional.

### Does it run on Mac or Linux?

Yes, with Docker. On Windows, the installer is the simpler option.

### Why do I need to create a Google Cloud credential?

Because seowatcher connects to Google directly from your computer, Google needs to know which Cloud project the requests come from. You set it up once per installation.

### Do I need to expose the app to the internet?

No. The app listens only on your own computer. If you want to reach it from elsewhere, put your own authentication in front of it.

## Where to start

1. [Install on Windows](https://seowatcher.io/en/docs/install-windows/) or [install with Docker](https://seowatcher.io/en/docs/install-docker/).
2. [Connect to Google](https://seowatcher.io/en/docs/google-connection/).
3. Optionally, the [PageSpeed key](https://seowatcher.io/en/docs/pagespeed-key/) and [agent setup](https://seowatcher.io/en/docs/agent-setup/).

---

# Install on Windows

URL: https://seowatcher.io/en/docs/install-windows/

> Install seowatcher on Windows 10 or 11 with one file, then update, repair, back up, change the port or uninstall it. No Docker needed.

The Windows package installs seowatcher for your user account and opens it in your browser. Installation takes about two minutes and needs no administrator rights, unless Windows is missing the Visual C++ runtime.

The app's interface is available in six languages; change it under **Settings → Appearance**. The tray menu is in Turkish only, so this guide gives each tray item in Turkish with its English meaning in brackets.

## What you need

- Windows 10 or 11 (64-bit).
- About 400 MB of free space. The installer file is 86 MB and the installed app is 313 MB.
- A browser such as Edge, Chrome or Firefox.
- No Docker, Node or terminal.
- Microsoft's Visual C++ runtime. If it is missing, the installer adds it and asks for administrator permission once.

## Steps

### First install

1. Download **seowatcher-setup.exe** from the GitHub releases page. The fixed address is: `github.com/ucsahinn/seotracker/releases/latest/download/seowatcher-setup.exe`
2. Double-click the file.
3. If Windows says "Windows protected your PC", click **More info**, then **Run anyway**. The installer is not code-signed yet, so Windows does not recognize the publisher; the warning is expected.
4. Optionally, compare the file's SHA-256 hash (the file's fingerprint) with `SHA256SUMS.txt` on the releases page.
5. In the installer wizard, go through the pages in this order:
   1. The welcome page: click **Next**.
   2. The "install for" page: choose **Install for me only**. This is the recommended per-user install, into `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\seowatcher`. **Install for all users** installs into `C:\Program Files\seowatcher` and asks for administrator permission.
   3. The options page: **Start seowatcher when Windows starts** (Turkish: "Windows açılınca seowatcher'ı başlat") and **Create a desktop shortcut** (Turkish: "Masaüstüne kısayol ekle"). The first one is checked by default. Clear it if you do not want the app to start in the background. Click **Next**.
   4. Click **Install** (on a Turkish Windows: **Kur**).
   5. The final page has a **Start seowatcher now** checkbox. Leave it checked and click **Finish** (on a Turkish Windows: **Bitti**). The app opens.
6. Wait 20-30 seconds for the first launch. The seowatcher icon appears in the notification area at the right end of the taskbar; if you cannot see it, click the ^ arrow there. The icon's text then changes in turn to "Anahtarlar hazırlanıyor" (Preparing keys), "Veritabanı güncelleniyor" (Updating database) and "Sunucu başlatılıyor" (Starting server). When it is ready, your browser opens by itself. When Windows starts it automatically, the browser does not open; a "seowatcher hazır" (seowatcher is ready) balloon appears instead.
7. `http://127.0.0.1:3001` opens in the browser by itself. This is your computer's own address (127.0.0.1) followed by the port number (3001).

Next, follow [Connecting to Google](https://seowatcher.io/en/docs/google-connection/).

### Taskbar menu

Right-click the tray icon to open the menu. From top to bottom it holds: opening the app and the status line, update and restart, the startup and update settings, and the troubleshooting items.

- **seowatcher'ı aç** (Open seowatcher): opens the app in the browser. Double-clicking the icon does the same. If the app is still starting, a "seowatcher açılıyor" (seowatcher is starting) balloon appears, and the browser opens by itself when it is ready.
- Status line: "Çalışıyor: http://127.0.0.1:3001/" (Running: http://127.0.0.1:3001/), "Veritabanı güncelleniyor" (Updating database) or an error text. It cannot be clicked. If the text is long, hold the mouse over it to see all of it.
- **Eksik Windows bileşenini kur** (Install the missing Windows component): shown only if the Visual C++ package is missing. When you click it, it installs the package and restarts the app.
- **Güncelle** (Update): always in the menu. Click it to check GitHub right away; if there is a new version it downloads and installs it, otherwise it says "Güncel" (up to date). While it checks, the item reads "Kontrol ediliyor…" (Checking…), and while it downloads it reads "Güncelleme indiriliyor: X.Y.Z (%45)" (Downloading update: X.Y.Z (45%)); it cannot be clicked then. When a new version has already been found, the item reads "Güncelle: X.Y.Z sürümü hazır" (Update: version X.Y.Z is ready); the version numbers are examples.
- **Yeniden başlat** (Restart): closes the app and opens it again. If something gets stuck, try this first.
- **Windows açılınca başlat** (Start with Windows): if checked, the app starts in the background when the computer starts. If an administrator turned this setting on during an install for all users of the computer, the item is checked and greyed out, and only an administrator can turn it off.
- **Güncellemeleri kendiliğinden kur** (Install updates automatically): if checked, the app installs a new version by itself when it finds one.
- **Windows bildirimleri** (Windows notifications): on by default. Shows finished and failed audits and new announcements as Windows notifications, even when the browser is closed. See [Settings](https://seowatcher.io/en/docs/settings/) for details.
- **Kurulumu onar** (Repair installation): clears temporary files, checks that the package is complete and reopens the app. While it repairs, the item reads "Onarılıyor…" (Repairing…).
- **Tanı bilgisini kopyala** (Copy diagnostic info): copies the Windows version, the processor, the Visual C++ version, a test run of the engine, the faulty module from the Windows event log, crash dumps and the last log lines to the clipboard. The information is ready in a few seconds, then a "Kopyalandı" (Copied) balloon appears. This helps when you report a problem.
- **Sorunu bildir (GitHub)** (Report a problem (GitHub)): puts the same information on the clipboard and opens a pre-filled issue on GitHub. Add one sentence about what you did and send it.
- **Günlükleri aç** (Open logs): opens the log folder. It holds `launcher.log`, `server.log` and `migrate.log`.
- **Veri klasörünü aç** (Open data folder): opens the folder with the database and the keys.
- Version number: the installed version. It cannot be clicked.
- **Çıkış** (Exit): closes the app completely. While it is closed, the page in the browser does not work.

If you start the app a second time (from the Start menu or the desktop shortcut), a second copy does not open. The app that is already open opens the page in the browser; if it is not ready yet, it opens the page when it is.

If the server closes by itself while running, the app reopens it and shows a "seowatcher yeniden başlatılıyor" (seowatcher is restarting) balloon. If it closes three times in ten minutes, the app stops reopening it and the status line reads "Sunucu 10 dakikada üç kez kapandı" (The server closed three times in 10 minutes). Then click **Kurulumu onar** (Repair installation).

### Update

The app updates itself. Two minutes after it opens, and once every day, it checks GitHub for the latest version. If there is a new version, it downloads it, compares the file's fingerprint (SHA-256) with the value on the releases page, then installs it silently and reopens. During this the icon text reads "Güncelleme indiriliyor" (Downloading update) and "Güncelleme kuruluyor" (Installing update), and a small installer window shows briefly. When the app reopens, a "seowatcher X.Y.Z sürümüne güncellendi" (seowatcher was updated to version X.Y.Z) balloon appears; click it to open the list of what is new. The **Settings → About** section inside the app also tells you about the new version and points you to **Güncelle** (Update) on the icon.

- If you do not want it to install by itself, clear **Güncellemeleri kendiliğinden kur** (Install updates automatically) in the menu. Then, when a new version comes out, you see a balloon once, and the menu item reads "Güncelle: X.Y.Z sürümü hazır" (Update: version X.Y.Z is ready). Click the balloon or the item to install.
- If there is no internet connection, or GitHub does not answer at that moment, the app tries again an hour later. For automatic attempts, it warns only once per version.
- If the downloaded file's fingerprint does not match, the update is not installed and the installed version keeps running.
- An install for all users of the computer needs administrator permission to update, so the app does not install by itself there. When a new version comes out you see a balloon; when you click it, Windows asks for administrator permission.
- To update by hand, download the new installer from the same address and run it. The wizard closes the running app, replaces the files and starts it again. The wizard's **Start seowatcher when Windows starts** checkbox reflects your current setting.

Your data, your Google connection and your settings stay as they are. An automatic update does not touch the **Windows açılınca başlat** (Start with Windows) setting.

### Company deployment

For IT teams that want to install for all users of a computer, or install silently with a deployment tool (Intune, GPO, PDQ):

- **For all users**: run the installer as administrator and choose the "all users" option in the wizard. The app installs under `C:\Program Files\seowatcher` (the per-user install goes to `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\seowatcher`). Each user's data still stays in their own `%LOCALAPPDATA%\seowatcher` folder.
- **Silent install**: `seowatcher-setup.exe /VERYSILENT /NORESTART` (single user) or `seowatcher-setup.exe /VERYSILENT /ALLUSERS /NORESTART` (administrator, all users). When a silent install finishes, the app opens by itself.
- **Install log**: every install writes to `%LOCALAPPDATA%\seowatcher\logs\setup.log`. You can give another place with `/LOG="path"`.
- **Silent uninstall**: `unins000.exe /VERYSILENT` (in the install folder: `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\seowatcher` for a per-user install, `C:\Program Files\seowatcher` for all users).
- **Verification**: before each version is published, it is installed on a clean Windows machine, opened, left running until the health address responds, and uninstalled. A version is not published until this test passes.

### Repair

If something gets stuck, right-click the tray icon and click **Kurulumu onar** (Repair installation). The app clears temporary files and checks that the package is complete. When it then opens, it runs the database update again.

If a file has been deleted from the package (for example, an antivirus program quarantined it), the app downloads the installer of the installed version from GitHub, verifies its fingerprint and reinstalls itself. Your data is not touched. If there is no internet connection, it says "Kurulum eksik" (Installation incomplete) and opens the releases page; then download the installer and run it.

### Uninstall

1. In Windows, open **Settings → Apps → Installed apps** and find **seowatcher**.
2. Click **Uninstall**.

The uninstaller removes the program, the Start menu shortcut, the "start with Windows" entry (including one you turned on from the menu) and downloaded update files. It does not touch the data folder, and the uninstall window says so too. If you also want to delete your database, your Google connection and your reports, delete the data folder yourself.

### Where is the data and how do I back it up?

Everything is in one folder: `%LOCALAPPDATA%\seowatcher`. Type this into the File Explorer address bar. The **Veri klasörünü aç** (Open data folder) menu item goes there too. It holds:

- `data`: the database (projects, the Search Console archive, audits, reports).
- `instance-secret`: the key that encrypts the Google access keys. If it is lost, you must set up the Google connections again from scratch.
- `mcp-token`: the password your AI assistant uses when it connects to the app.
- `server.env`, `config.json`, `logs`.

To make a backup:

1. Close the app with **Çıkış** (Exit).
2. Copy the whole folder.

To restore, close the app, put the folder back in place and start the app. Moving to another computer works the same way. If you take the `instance-secret` file too, the Google connections keep working.

### Changing the port number

The app uses port 3001. If another program holds it, the app picks the first free number from 3002 to 3010, but only for that one start, and shows a "3001 numarası dolu, 3002 kullanılıyor" (Port 3001 is in use, using 3002) balloon. It does not save this number. When 3001 is free again, the app uses 3001 on the next start, because the redirect addresses at Google contain this number.

To choose a specific port:

1. Close the app.
2. Open the `config.json` file in the data folder with Notepad.
3. Write this in it:

```json
{
  "port": 3005
}
```

4. Save it and start the app. If the file has other lines (such as `autoUpdate`), do not delete them; change only the value of `port`.

If you use an OAuth client, update its two redirect URIs at Google to the new port. See [Connecting to Google](https://seowatcher.io/en/docs/google-connection/).

## Check

- Hovering over the tray icon shows "seowatcher X.Y.Z: Çalışıyor: http://127.0.0.1:3001/" (Running), where X.Y.Z is the version you installed.
- In the browser, the address `http://127.0.0.1:3001/api/health` should show a text that starts with "status":"ok".
- On the **Help** screen, the **App health** card shows no problems except **Google sign-in**, which asks for attention until you connect Google.

## Frequently asked questions

**Why does it open in the browser?** The app runs on your computer like a small server. The browser is its screen.

**What happens when I turn off the computer?** The app closes too. If **Windows açılınca başlat** (Start with Windows) is checked, it starts by itself the next time the computer starts.

**Can I open it from another computer?** No, and this is on purpose. The app listens only on the 127.0.0.1 address. To open it to the internet, you need to put your own authentication in front of it.

**Can I switch from the Docker version?** Yes, but the data does not move by itself. You need to create the projects and connect Google again. The Search Console archive refills from Google's last 16 months when you open Search performance or Rank tracking.

**My antivirus gave a warning.** Some antivirus programs warn because the file is unsigned. Download the file only from the GitHub releases page and compare its SHA-256 hash.

## If something goes wrong

- **The icon says "Hata: 3001 ve sonraki 9 adres numarası (port) dolu" (Error: 3001 and the next 9 ports are in use).** Another program holds these numbers. Write another number in the `config.json` file.
- **The icon says "Veritabanı güncellemesi başarısız" (Database update failed).** Click **Günlükleri aç** (Open logs) and check the last lines of `migrate.log`. Usually the disk is full or the folder is read-only.
- **The icon says "Sunucu beklenmedik şekilde kapandı" (The server closed unexpectedly) or "Sunucu 10 dakikada üç kez kapandı" (The server closed three times in 10 minutes).** The last lines of `server.log` give the reason. Try **Yeniden başlat** (Restart), and if that does not help, **Kurulumu onar** (Repair installation). If it still does not help, click **Sorunu bildir (GitHub)** (Report a problem (GitHub)).
- **The icon says "Veritabanı güncellemesi 15 dakikada bitmedi" (The database update did not finish in 15 minutes).** Another program may have locked the database file (a backup or sync program). Stop that program and click **Yeniden başlat** (Restart).
- **The browser did not open.** Double-click the icon or type the address by hand: `http://127.0.0.1:3001`

---

# Install with Docker

URL: https://seowatcher.io/en/docs/install-docker/

> Run seowatcher in Docker on Mac, Linux or Windows with one command, then update, back up, configure or remove it.

Docker runs seowatcher in a container at `http://localhost:3001`. Use it on Mac and Linux, or on Windows if you already work with Docker; otherwise the [Windows installer](https://seowatcher.io/en/docs/install-windows/) is simpler.

## What you need

- Docker Desktop (Mac, Windows) or Docker Engine with Docker Compose (Linux).
- On Windows, Docker Desktop also needs WSL 2 and virtualization enabled in the BIOS/UEFI.
- Git. If you do not have it, **Code → Download ZIP** on the GitHub page also works.
- About 2 GB of free disk space, and 2 GB of free memory during the first build.

## Steps

1. Download the repository (the project files) and go into its folder:

```sh
git clone https://github.com/ucsahinn/seotracker.git
cd seotracker
```

2. Start the app:

```sh
docker compose up -d
```

No `.env` file is needed. The encryption key and the assistant token are created on first start and stored in the data volume.

3. To follow the progress, run:

```sh
docker compose logs -f
```

4. Wait. The log line "Building client + server" marks the first build. Wait until `docker compose ps` shows the status **healthy**, then open `http://localhost:3001` in the browser.

Next, follow [Connecting to Google](https://seowatcher.io/en/docs/google-connection/). If you use an OAuth client on Docker, its two redirect URIs are:

- `http://localhost:3001/api/gsc/oauth/callback`
- `http://localhost:3001/api/ga4/oauth/callback`

### Updating

Run these two commands:

```sh
git pull
docker compose up -d --build
```

**Settings → About** tells you about the new version and shows these two commands. Your data stays in the data volume named `seotracker_data`, so updating does not delete it.

### Stopping and removing

- To stop: `docker compose stop`
- To start again: `docker compose up -d`
- To remove the container and keep the data: `docker compose down`
- To delete the data too: `docker compose down -v`. This command permanently deletes the database, the Google connections and the reports.

### Backing up

Your data is in the `seotracker_data` volume, at the path `/app/.wrangler` inside the container. To make a backup, run these three commands in order:

```sh
docker compose stop
docker run --rm -v seotracker_data:/data -v "$PWD":/backup alpine tar czf /backup/seotracker-yedek.tgz -C /data .
docker compose up -d
```

To restore, use `tar xzf` instead of `tar czf` in the same command. The `instance-secret` file in the data volume is the key that encrypts the Google connections. A backup that lacks it restores without the Google connections.

### Settings (optional)

No setting is required. To change something, put a `.env` file in the project folder and then run `docker compose up -d --force-recreate seotracker`.

| Setting name                           | What it does                                                                                                                                 |
| -------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| PORT                                   | The port number, 3001 by default. When it changes, the Google redirect addresses change too                                                  |
| ALLOWED_HOST                           | The public host name, if the app runs behind another server. If empty, only localhost                                                        |
| AUTH_MODE                              | `local_noauth` (default) or `cloudflare_access`                                                                                              |
| BETTER_AUTH_SECRET                     | The encryption key. Leave it empty and the app creates one. If you set it by hand, use at least 32 characters and never change it afterwards |
| GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID, GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET | An alternative to entering them on the **Settings** screen. A value entered on the screen takes priority                                     |
| PAGESPEED_API_KEY                      | An alternative to entering it on the **Settings** screen                                                                                     |
| MCP_TOKEN                              | The assistant token. If empty, one is created on first start. `off` disables the token check. Any other value is used as the token           |

## Check

- In the output of `docker compose ps`, the status should be **healthy**. On the first start, it can take up to five minutes to get there.
- The output of `curl.exe http://127.0.0.1:3001/api/health` should start with "status":"ok". You can also open `http://127.0.0.1:3001/api/health` in the browser.
- `http://localhost:3001` opens in the browser. On the **Help** screen, the **App health** card shows no problems except **Google sign-in**, which asks for attention until you connect Google.

## Frequently asked questions

**Why is the first start long?** The app is built inside the container. On later starts, the build is skipped.

**Where is the `.env.example` file?** There is none. That file, inherited from the upstream project, described things that are not in this version. The full list is in the table above and in the `docs/ENVIRONMENT.md` file.

**Can I open it to the internet?** The app does not ask who you are, so do not open it to the internet without your own authentication in front of it. If you set `ALLOWED_HOST`, the app warns you in the health check.

**Where do I get my assistant's token?** The **Agent setup** screen shows the command: `docker compose exec -T seotracker cat /app/.wrangler/mcp-token`. If you use Git Bash, put `MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1` in front of the command.

## If something goes wrong

- **It says "Bind for 127.0.0.1:3001 failed".** The port number is in use. Put a `.env` file with the line `PORT=3002` in the project folder and recreate the container. On Windows, Notepad may save the file as `.env.txt`; in PowerShell, `Set-Content -Encoding ascii .env 'PORT=3002'` avoids that.
- **The status is "unhealthy".** `docker compose logs --tail 50` shows the last lines. If memory ran out during the build, give Docker Desktop more memory.
- **The Google connection says it "isn't configured".** If `BETTER_AUTH_SECRET` is shorter than 32 characters, Google stays off. If you set it by hand, make it longer. If you did not, the `instance-secret` file in the data volume may be damaged.
- **The Google connection dropped after an update.** `BETTER_AUTH_SECRET` changed, or the data volume was recreated. Choose **Reconnect** in the project settings.

---

# Connecting to Google

URL: https://seowatcher.io/en/docs/google-connection/

> Give seowatcher read access to Search Console and GA4 with your own service account or OAuth client, then choose a property per project.

seowatcher runs on your computer and talks to Google directly, so it needs a credential from your own Google Cloud project. You can use a service account or an OAuth client. The credential is saved once for the whole installation; each project then gets its own Search Console property and GA4 property.

## Two scopes: credential and property

| Setting                         | Where                                                   | Applies to             |
| ------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------- |
| Service account or OAuth client | **Settings → Service account** or **Settings → Google** | The whole installation |
| Search Console and GA4 property | **Project settings → Connections**                      | One project            |

"Saved" means the credential is stored. A selected property means the project is bound to it. Neither proves that Google will return report data; you know access works when **Search performance** or **Analytics** shows data. Selecting a GA4 property does not install a tracking tag on your site.

If both a service account and an OAuth client are saved, the service account is used.

## Option 1: service account

A service account needs no sign-in flow and does not expire, which makes it the shorter route.

1. In Google Cloud Console, enable the **Google Search Console API**. For Analytics, also enable the **Google Analytics Admin API** and the **Google Analytics Data API**.
2. Create a service account and download its JSON key file.
3. In seowatcher, open **Settings → Service account**. Select the JSON file, or paste its contents into the masked field, and save. The private key is never shown again.
4. Copy the service account email address the app displays. Add it as a user in Search Console with **Full** permission, and in Google Analytics with the **Viewer** role.
5. In each project, open **Project settings → Connections** and choose the property.

## Option 2: OAuth client

1. In Google Cloud Console, create an OAuth client of type **Web application**.
2. Add both redirect URIs shown in **Settings → Google**, character for character. They are built from the address you opened the app at, for example `http://127.0.0.1:3001/api/gsc/oauth/callback` and `http://127.0.0.1:3001/api/ga4/oauth/callback`. `localhost` and `127.0.0.1` count as different addresses.
3. Save the client ID and client secret in **Settings → Google**.
4. In each project, open **Project settings → Connections**, select **Add Google account**, grant access and choose the property.

While the OAuth consent screen is in **Testing**, only the accounts listed as test users can sign in, and Google can expire the grant after seven days. Publish the consent screen or use a service account to avoid reconnecting.

## When something fails

- **Property list did not refresh.** The previous list stays visible. An empty list on its own does not prove missing access.
- **Expired grant.** Select **Reconnect** in the project's connections.
- **Access denied.** Check the account's permission on the property.
- **API disabled.** Enable the API in the Google Cloud project.
- **Rate limit.** Wait and try again.
- **Unknown error.** Select **Try again**, then check the [Help](https://seowatcher.io/en/docs/help/) screen and its diagnostics bundle.

The connection card shows the date of the last successful Google read for the current credential and property, and for GA4 the property's time zone and currency. After a temporary failure it keeps that date. If there is no successful read yet, access is unverified. Opening the settings screen does not query Google.

Removing a credential from seowatcher does not revoke it at Google. A new credential does not inherit the previous one's access or quota history, so refresh the reports after switching. Changing a project's domain keeps its property binding and its stored history.

---

# PageSpeed key

URL: https://seowatcher.io/en/docs/pagespeed-key/

> Create a free PageSpeed Insights API key, save it in Settings, test it and read the quota counters shown during site audits.

The site audit measures page speed with Google PageSpeed Insights. The API key is free and optional. Without one, the app measures at most 50 pages per audit, and Google often stops keyless requests early with a 429 (too many requests) error. Crawling and the other checks do not need a key.

## Create and save a key

1. In Google Cloud Console, enable the **PageSpeed Insights API**.
2. Create an API key and restrict it to the PageSpeed Insights API.
3. In seowatcher, open **Settings → Speed tests**, paste the key and select **Save**.

The app stores the key encrypted and never shows it again. On Docker you can set `PAGESPEED_API_KEY` instead; a key saved in Settings takes priority.

## Test the key

**Test key** sends one real mobile request for example.com. It does not measure your site and does not count toward the audit counter. The result and the test date appear next to the button. The button stays disabled while the test runs and for at least ten seconds after you select it. Saving a different key clears the old test result.

A successful test proves only that this one request worked. A key does not guarantee that every audit request succeeds; check your actual quota in Google Cloud Console.

## Quota counters

The PageSpeed counter under **Settings → Google and system limits** counts the measurements of audits started in the last 24 hours. It excludes key tests and any other program that uses the same key.

## Fix a failing key

| Result                     | What to do                                                                      |
| -------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Invalid key                | Copy the key again from Google Cloud Console and save it.                       |
| 403 or "restricted"        | Check that the API is enabled and that the key's restrictions allow it.         |
| 429 or daily quota reached | Wait for the quota to reset, then check the quota page in Google Cloud Console. |
| Network error              | Check the internet connection and test again.                                   |

---

# Projects

URL: https://seowatcher.io/en/docs/projects/

> Create a project for each site, pick the one to work on, finish its connections and archive or restore projects without losing data.

A project is one site. It keeps its own Search Console property, GA4 property, audits, reports and notes. The **Projects** screen lists them, shows what each one still needs and takes you to its next step.

## Find and open a project

With several projects, search by name or domain and sort by either. **Last opened** marks the project this browser opened most recently; it says nothing about the site's health. Each card offers the next useful action for that project: **Add site**, **Connect Search Console** or **Open dashboard**. **Project context** opens the project's notes and **Settings** opens its configuration.

## What a project card shows

**Search archive** shows clicks from the locally stored Search Console archive: Web search, all devices and all countries. The dates are on the card. The window ends on the newest stored day, which can be some time ago if the archive has not been updated. If days are missing, the click count covers only the days that were observed; a missing day is a gap, not zero. A change is shown only when both periods are complete. Equal totals read **No change**.

When the previous period has fewer than 20 clicks, the badge shows the difference in clicks instead of a percentage. A rise from 1 to 5 clicks reads +4 clicks; a change that small is not evidence of growth on its own. A rise from zero shows both counts.

The audit summary belongs to the project's own domain. The last completed audit and a newer attempt that is still running or failed are shown separately.

A saved connection does not prove that Google data can be read. If a source cannot be read, the card says so instead of showing it as disconnected or as zero; use **Try again**. Refreshing the screen reads local data only. It does not call Google and does not start an audit.

## Create a project

Choose **New project** and enter a name. Domain, country and language are optional. Creating a project collects no data. Next, open **Project settings → Connections** and choose one Search Console property and one GA4 property for the project. The **Basics** tab changes the name, domain and market.

## Archive and restore

Archiving hides a project and keeps all its data. Restore it from the **Archived** list. You cannot archive your only project.

## Comparing projects

Search Console clicks, GA4 sessions and archive totals measure different things, so do not compare one project's clicks with another project's sessions. Cards can also cover different dates; do not add them together.

---

# Dashboard

URL: https://seowatcher.io/en/docs/dashboard/

> The project's starting screen: Google search totals, the next few tasks worth doing, the latest audit and organic traffic from GA4.

The **Dashboard** summarizes one project on a single screen: search results from Search Console, up to three next tasks, the latest site audit and organic traffic from Google Analytics. Each card states the dates and the source it covers.

**Refresh** reads the dashboard sources, the setup status and the Google configuration again. If one source fails, the dashboard reports a partial refresh and keeps the rest. The time the data was retrieved is shown separately from the latest day the data covers.

## Search summary

The default view is the last 28 complete days of Web search, all devices and all countries, on Google's Pacific calendar. Recent days that Google has not finalized are left out. The source line shows the exact current and previous dates, the latest data day and the excluded days; if Google gives no finality date, the screen says it is assuming one.

- **Clicks**: visits from Google search results.
- **Impressions**: times your site appeared in results.
- **CTR**: clicks divided by impressions.
- **Average position**: weighted by impressions; lower is better, and 1 is the top.

Each tile opens **Search performance** with the same settings. The faded line on the daily click chart is the previous period. A rise from zero shows the absolute count instead of a percentage; a fall to zero shows a normal negative percentage. If the previous period is missing, no change is shown.

When the previous period has too few clicks for a reliable comparison, the summary leads with the actual clicks and impressions. With little data, a percentage alone does not show growth or decline.

## Next tasks

Up to three tasks come from connection problems, audit findings, search opportunities or an outdated audit. A connected source alone does not create a task, and a failed audit read never turns into first-use advice. An empty task list means nothing urgent was found in the data that could be read; it does not certify that every source is healthy.

## Setup

The **Setup checklist** uses the same six signals as [Project context](https://seowatcher.io/en/docs/project-context/) and reports a missing signal separately from an unreadable one. A completed audit of the project's own domain counts as outdated after seven days. **Setup preferences** is an optional, collapsed tour with no score of its own. Steps you put off can be brought back once no active step remains.

## Queries that could move up one position band

This card lists queries with a rounded average position from 4 to 20 and enough impressions. The extra clicks shown assume each query moves up one position band. They are an upper bound, not measured traffic. Queries with and without an estimate are counted across the whole eligible set before the top four are shown; if no estimate is possible, the card does not show zero. The card also states whether brand queries were separated using confirmed names, suggested names or not at all.

An empty card does not mean no query ranks between 4 and 20: the impression threshold scales with the period, and brand queries are excluded. Do not add this estimate to the total on [Opportunities](https://seowatcher.io/en/docs/opportunities/), which counts pages over a different period.

## Site audit

The card uses only audits of the project's own domain; a newer audit of a different site is ignored. It shows the last completed audit and, separately, any newer audit that is still running or failed. If the project has no domain, the card links to project settings. Otherwise it names the start URL, date, measured checks and any page limit.

The counts use different units: affected pages, failed check types and severity counts per page and check. One page can fail three checks. Info findings sit outside the critical and warning bar. Health wording applies only to what was measured; a page limit or unmeasured checks mean the result does not cover the whole site.

Changes between audits appear only when both audits share the same start URL, settings and crawled pages and have usable measurements. A check counts as fixed only if it was measured in both audits. **Pages with the most issues** opens the same audit's issues, filtered to the selected URL.

## Organic traffic

Organic sessions, active users, engagement rate and key events come from Google Analytics, with the dates and the property's time zone shown. Sessions are not the same as Google clicks and include other search engines. An unknown or restricted value never means zero traffic; the other readable values stay visible. Privacy thresholds, sampling and access limits are named on the card, unreliable comparisons are withheld, and missing days stay as gaps. If sessions are unknown, check the source warnings in the [Analytics](https://seowatcher.io/en/docs/analytics/) report, the connection's access and the site's tag.

Revenue and orders stay visible if either period has recorded sales, even when the current period is zero. If neither period has sales data, the note under **Organic revenue** says sales measurement is unverified. An unknown currency is labelled.

## What the dashboard does not include

There is no keyword volume, backlink data or competitor ranking. To compare a figure with Google's own reports, use the same dates and filters there.

---

# Search performance

URL: https://seowatcher.io/en/docs/search-performance/

> Clicks, impressions, CTR and position from Search Console, with a ranked to-do list, changes, overlaps and the queries behind every page.

**Search performance** shows how your site appears in Google Search and what to work on first. Clicks, impressions, CTR and position come straight from Search Console; the app estimates nothing except the possible-gain figures, which are always labelled as an upper bound.

The filters you choose are stored in the URL, so you can bookmark or share a view.

## Three terms

**Final day.** Search Console keeps counting a day for several days. Totals and comparisons use only days whose count has finished. Days follow the Pacific time Google uses. Days that are still being counted show hatched on the chart.

**Hidden query.** Google does not list very rarely searched queries, for privacy. But it adds their clicks to the site total. That is why the query table adds up to less than the site total. The difference is the hidden queries.

**Upper bound.** A gain figure means "at most this much". It is the extra clicks a search would get if it rose one step, at your own site's click-through rates. The real result depends on competitors and on Google, and is usually smaller.

## What is on the screen

**Top bar.** At the top right:

- **Refresh**: asks Search Console for fresh data. The app normally reuses an answer up to ten minutes old; **Refresh** skips that cache.
- **Download report**: turns the view on screen into a printable one-file report, saves it and downloads it. The report also sits in the **Reports** screen.
- The export menu: **Queries (CSV)**, **Pages (CSV)**, **Queries close to the top three (CSV)**, **Export queries to Sheets**, **Export pages to Sheets**. Exports follow the filters on screen. If you have a search or a quick filter on the Queries or Pages tab, it carries into the file too.

**Filters.** A one-line bar summarises the chosen filters: "(Web, All devices, All countries, Last 28 days, Against previous period)". Open it to see: **Search type** (Web, Image, Video, News), **Device filter** (All devices, Mobile, Desktop, Tablet), **Country filter** (the countries Google reports for that period), **Date range** (Last 7 days, Last 28 days, Last 3 months) and **Comparison** (Against previous period, Against last year, No comparison).

**Data status.** A strip that states what the numbers are based on. For example "Data is final up to 24 Oct; the last 3 days are still being counted (hatched on the chart)." The same strip shows which days the comparison uses and the name of your Search Console property. Press the property name to go to the project's connection settings. If last year's comparison is chosen and Google no longer gives those days, the strip says so (Google goes back 16 months at most). Open **About the data** to see: the date of the final days, how many days are still being counted and the last data date, the share of clicks from hidden queries, whether the tables were read in full (Google returns a limited number of rows at a time) and whether this view sent new requests to Google or used an answer taken a few minutes ago.

**Summary sentence.** A sentence or two above the tiles says what happened. For example "Clicks rose 6.1% in the last 28 days against the previous period. CTR fell 0.3 points." Then it says how many extra clicks the first three jobs could bring together, marked "(upper bound)". The **To do** link takes you to that tab.

**Four tiles.** **Clicks**, **Impressions**, **CTR** (what percentage of impressions were clicked) and **Average position**. All are totals of the final days. Each tile shows the change against the comparison you chose, and a small line. The change in clicks and impressions is written as a percentage, in CTR as points and in position as places. For average position, a small number is good, and 1 is the top spot. The direction of a change is shown with an arrow as well as colour.

**Over time chart.** It draws the daily values.

- The picker at the top right switches between four measures: clicks, impressions, CTR and average position. On the position chart, up is a better position.
- The **Day**, **Week** and **Month** buttons change the time unit. The comparison line (a dashed line) appears only in the day view.
- The hatched area is days Google is still counting. A hollow dot means an incomplete or not yet final period.
- Numbered markers above the line show three things: ranking updates Google announced ("Google update"), the days site audits finished ("Site audit completed") and your own notes. Under the chart, each number is explained.
- **Add a note** leaves your own note on a date, for example "New page titles went live". A note is at most 280 characters. It helps you remember later why something dropped or rose. Notes outside the chosen period are collected under "Notes outside this period (N)".

**Start with these strip.** Between the chart and the tabs, the first three to-dos sit side by side. Each has its title, its possible gain and a button. **All to-dos (N)** takes you to the To do tab.

**Tabs.** There are seven: **To do (N)**, **Queries (N)**, **Pages (N)**, **Ranking opportunities (N)**, **Changes**, **Overlaps** and **Distribution**. The number in brackets is the count of rows or findings inside the tab. If queries or pages are falling, the Changes tab reads "Changes (N falling)". When you switch tabs, the search box and the quick filter reset.

### To do

The app ranks the jobs it finds in Search Console data by estimated gain. Jobs are grouped by kind, and each group's heading says how many jobs it holds:

- "N queries close to the top three": searches with an average position between 4 and 20 and enough impressions. Brand searches are left out of this list. Strengthen the page for that search.
- "N results get few clicks for their position": searches clicked less than your site's other searches at the same position. Rewrite the title and description.
- "Clicks fell for N queries" and "Clicks fell for N pages": a clear drop against the previous period. If the position fell too, update the content. If the position held, review the title and description.
- "N pages are losing their old strength": pages that fell far below the best of the previous four quarters in the last quarter. Refresh the page.
- "N pages are seen but never clicked". The gain estimate here is cautious: it uses the click-through rate of the position band below the page's own, not its own band. Pages on page two or further back get no estimate.
- "You no longer appear for N queries": searches that got clicks in the previous period and no impressions now.
- "You trail on N device types" and "You trail in N countries".
- "Unusual drops on N days": that day's clicks or impressions were unusually low against the same weekday in earlier weeks.
- "Set your brand name": appears when no brand name is set, so brand searches can be separated. When the app is splitting them with names it suggested from your domain, the job reads "Confirm your brand name" instead. Confirm the suggestions if they are right, or enter your brand's name.

In each group's heading, **Why, and what to do** gives the reason and what to do. A row shows its rank number, the finding, the evidence (for example "Position 8.2 · 640 impressions · 12 clicks"), the possible gain written as "≈ +N clicks" and a confidence label (**Confidence: high**, medium or low). The first four jobs of a group are shown, and **Show all (N)** opens the rest.

Mark a job finished with **Done**. Marked jobs go under "Marked as done (N)" and come back with **Restore**. The done marks are kept only in this browser. **Details** (or **Open this breakdown**) on a row opens the detail of that search, page, device or country. If there are several jobs for one search or page, the total at the top counts it once.

### Queries and Pages

A table of queries or pages. The columns are **Query** (or **Page**), **Clicks**, **Click change** (against the comparison), **Impressions**, **CTR** and **Position**. Click a heading to sort. The bar behind a row is its share of the clicks in this table. The box at the top searches among the rows. Beside it, "{shown} / {total} rows" is written.

**Quick filters.** For queries: **In the top 10**, **Position 4-10**, **Position 11-20**, **Low CTR**, **No clicks**. For pages: **In the top 10**, **Clicked**, **Low CTR**, **No clicks**. Low CTR means a row on page one with at least 100 impressions and a click-through below 2 percent.

**Row menu.** In the three dots: **Open page in a new tab**, **Copy URL**, **Copy keyword**, **Save as keyword**. What you save goes to the **Saved keywords** screen. Clicking a row opens the detail panel.

The note under the table gives the base: "read N queries, N clicks. The site total is N clicks; the difference comes from the queries Google hides." If Google's row limit was reached, the least-clicked end is missing from the list and the note says so.

### Ranking opportunities

There are four sections.

- **Queries close to the top three.** Searches with an average position between 4 and 20. Brand searches are not included. It says how many extra clicks they could bring together if each rose one step (from 6-10 to 4-5, from 4-5 to 2-3, from 11-20 to page one). That is an upper bound. The total covers every query in this range, not only the rows listed, and is followed by the dates it covers, for example "Period: Sep 27, 2026 – Oct 24, 2026." When only the largest gains are listed, a note below says "The N with the largest gain are listed." The table shows **Query**, **Target page**, **Position**, **Impressions**, **Clicks** and **Possible gain**. The target page is the page Google shows most for that search. You take the searches you select with **Copy keywords** or **Save as keyword**.
- **Results clicked less than their position suggests.** Searches whose click-through falls below 70 percent of your site's rate for results at the same position. The gain comes without any change in position, only by rewriting the title and description. The table shows the search's rate, the rate **Expected at this position** and the possible gain.
- **Pages that show up but never get clicked.** Pages that got at least 100 impressions (for 28 days) in the period and not one click.
- **Your site's CTR by position.** The yardstick for the gains above. It is the click-through rate of your own results at each position, not other sites'. If a position has too few searches or impressions, it says "Not enough data" and no estimate is made for it. If you defined brand names, these rates are calculated from non-brand searches.

### Changes

It compares the chosen period with the previous one.

- **Biggest changes since the previous period.** Two lists: **Falling (N)** and **Rising (N)**. For a search or page to enter a list, its clicks must move by at least 3 clicks and 20 percent of its previous value. Small moves do not enter. A row shows the previous and new clicks, impressions and position.
- **Newly showing** and **Lost (with their previous-period numbers).** Only searches that got at least 50 impressions (for 28 days) in just one period. If one period's table is incomplete because of the row limit, it cannot be known which search is new or lost, and the screen says so.
- **Pages losing ground.** Pages whose clicks in the last quarter (91 days) fell below 70 percent of the best of the previous four quarters, and are also behind the same quarter last year. This comparison needs more than a year of data. If Search Console did not give data that old, or a filter is on, the screen says so.
- **Long term: monthly clicks.** Search Console goes back 16 months. The app keeps the daily totals longer on this computer. The bars show monthly clicks. A bar with a dashed outline is a month the archive does not hold in full. If the archive is still filling, the screen says "No days in the archive yet" or gives the start date. This section follows the device filter, not the country filter.

### Overlaps

It shows cases where several of your pages appear for the same search. Pages can split each other's clicks. Most of the time it is enough to make one the main page and link to it from the others. The card's heading reads "Pages competing for one query".

- Three tiles: **Queries with competing pages**, **Impressions going to the other pages** and **Query losing the most**. Press the last tile and the list narrows to that query.
- The **Pages competing for the same query** table shows, for each query, its pages, their clicks, impressions and positions. The page Google shows most for that query counts as the "preferred" one. The share of impressions going to the others is written as "outside the share".
- This analysis looks at 28 days. If 7 days is chosen, it is raised to 28 for the analysis and the real date range is written. Only searches with at least 100 impressions are examined. For a page to join the contest, it needs at least 10 impressions and a 20 percent share on that search.
- If the search hits Search Console's row limit, the screen warns that some queries could not be examined.

### Distribution

- **Position distribution.** Shows in groups which positions your searches appear at. If the archive holds at least two weeks, **Queries by week** appears below it. This chart covers Web searches only. With Image, Video or News selected as the search type, it says "The weekly distribution is for Web searches only." in its place. That chart shows the share of the position groups week by week. It comes from the query archive on your computer. It is not shown with a device or country filter, because the archive does not keep those breakdowns.
- **Brand and non-brand searches.** Searches that arrive with your name and searches by people who did not know you are measured separately: **Brand searches** and **Non-brand searches**. For each, the number of queries, clicks, CTR and average position are written. If no brand name is defined, it says "Brand searches are not separated" and an **Add brand name** button appears. If the app suggested brand names from your domain, it says "Not confirmed." The measurement was then made with the suggested names. Press **Confirm suggestions** or use **Edit brand names**. Shares are of the queries read; hidden queries are not included.
- **Devices** and **Countries.** Click a device or country and the whole screen narrows to it.
- **Search appearance.** Which special formats your results show in on Google (rich results, video and so on). A rich result is a result that shows extra information such as a product or video. Google adds up this breakdown by page. If Google reported no special format, the screen says so.
- **Question searches.** Searches shaped as questions and searches of four or more words. They are the clearest source of content ideas.

**Brand names.** Enter brand names with **Edit brand names**. Enter your site's name and the ways people spell it, for example the name and its short form. Searches containing these words count as brand searches. There are **Save** and **Cancel** buttons, and the **Suggestions:** line adds a name in one click. Defining brand names changes not only this screen but also the gain estimate on the **Opportunities** screen, because that estimate leaves brand searches out.

**Detail panel.** Click a search or a page (in a table, in To do, in Ranking opportunities or in Changes) and it opens from the right. At the top it says the date range and "final days". Then come four numbers (Clicks, Impressions, CTR, Average position) and their change against the chosen comparison. Below is the **Daily clicks** line. For a page, a list "This page's queries (N)" appears; for a search, "Pages showing for this query (N)". Each row gives clicks and position. The listed queries can add up to less than the page's total, or be missing entirely: the difference is the queries Google hides. **Open page** opens the page in a new tab. **Save as keyword** adds the search to **Saved keywords**.

## Links from other screens

Links from **Opportunities** and **Rank tracking** open the exact page or query in the detail panel for the source dates. The tiles stay site-wide; the figures for the selected page or query are in the detail panel. If those dates cannot be read, the screen says so instead of quietly switching to other dates. Choosing a period preset clears dates set by a link.

**Download report** sends the dates on screen to the server and is unavailable while a refresh runs. The report keeps those dates, but Google may have revised the figures by the time it reads them again.

## How to use it

1. First read the summary sentence at the top. It says whether clicks are rising or falling.
2. Look at the **Start with these** strip or the **To do** tab. The first three jobs are the ones that gain the most.
3. If there is a big drop, set the **Date range** to **Last 3 months**. Find the day the drop began on the chart. If a Google update or a change you made falls on that day, it shows in the markers.
4. On the **Ranking opportunities** tab, look at **Queries close to the top three**. Open the page of the three most-shown searches. Adjust the title and first paragraph to that search.
5. On the **Queries** tab, press the **Low CTR** button. Your position is good but nobody clicks. The problem is most likely the title and description.
6. On the **Changes** tab, look at **Falling**. Click the top search and read the day the drop began in the detail panel.
7. If the **Overlaps** tab shows several of your pages competing for one query, decide which page should rank for it and point your internal links to that page.
8. After a fix, write its date on the chart with **Add a note**. Two weeks later you see its effect on the chart.
9. When a job is finished, mark it **Done**.
10. At the end of the month, save the view with **Download report**.

## How the numbers are calculated

Google reports data about three days late, and the most recent days can still change. The range therefore ends about three days ago, and days that are not final are left out of the totals. The previous period is the period of the same length right before this range. For the last-year comparison, the same days of last year are taken. You see the change in clicks and impressions as a percentage and the change in CTR as points.

The tiles are the real totals of the site. The tables count each page that appears for the same search separately. If you add up the page table, you get a larger number than the tile. That is not an error. If you add up the query table, you get a smaller number than the tile, because hidden queries are not listed.

The app reads the query, page and query-page tables in chunks of 25,000 rows until Google returns no new rows. Google serves at most 50,000 rows per day per search type and can skip some rows, so reading every chunk does not mean every search is known. If the limit was reached, the least-clicked end is missing and the screen says so. Site totals are not added up from these tables; they are a separate total from Google.

The app starts at most ten requests to Google per second. After a quota error from Google, new reads wait fifteen minutes. Sources: [Google's guide to getting all your data](https://developers.google.com/webmaster-tools/v1/how-tos/all-your-data), [API quotas](https://developers.google.com/webmaster-tools/limits).

**Possible gain.** The app applies your site's own click-through rate to each search. It takes the rate one step up from the position the search is at, multiplies it by the search's impressions and subtracts the current clicks. Searches with very few impressions do not count (at least 50 impressions for 28 days). For title problems, the yardstick is the search reaching your site's rate at the same position. Brand searches are left out. That is why every gain is an upper bound. The same calculation is used on the **Opportunities** screen.

**Confidence label.** The label beside each job shows how solid the data behind the finding is: high, medium or low.

**Small samples.** When the comparison period has too few clicks for a reliable analysis, the summary leads with the actual clicks and impressions. With little data, percentages and averages alone do not show growth or decline. An empty opportunity list does not mean no query ranks between 4 and 20: the impression threshold scales with the period, and brand queries are excluded. When the to-do list is empty, review the visible queries yourself. The app does not suggest a longer period when the last three months are already selected, and it does not assume Google will later reveal hidden queries.

## Questions

**My position is different when I search on Google.** The position here is the average over the period. It does not reflect a single search.

**The search I look for is not in the list.** Google hides very rarely searched queries. On small sites there may be no query rows at all.

**Why did a job vanish from the To do list?** If you marked it done, it is under "Marked as done". The marks are kept only in this browser. In another browser or on another computer you see it again.

**If pages overlap, should I merge them?** Usually not. Pick the page that should rank and link to it from the others. Merge pages only if they really answer the same question.

**Do I have to enter a brand name?** No, but if you do not, people searching for your own name distort the CTR calculation and the opportunities come out incomplete. The screen reminds you with the "Set your brand name" job. When the app is using names it suggested from your domain, the job reads "Confirm your brand name".

## Limits

The Discover and Google News search types are not included. There is no search volume and no competitor position. Data does not go back further than 16 months from Google. For older data, look at the archive on this computer: the long-term chart on the **Changes** tab and the **Rank tracking** screen read from it. The archive fills only while this screen or Rank tracking is open.

---

# Rank tracking

URL: https://seowatcher.io/en/docs/rank-tracking/

> Follow average Google positions for your Search Console queries over time, beyond Google's 16-month window, using the local archive.

**Rank tracking** reads the Search Console Web queries stored in the local archive. Because the archive lives on your computer, it keeps history that Google drops after 16 months.

Average position is not a fixed rank that every searcher sees; it varies with location, device and context. Impressions are not search volume.

## Risers and fallers

The summary compares two periods. It counts the queries observed in both periods that moved by at least half a position, and counts separately the queries that cannot be compared. Start with the history of the suggested faller. Priority is the change in position multiplied by the query's impressions; it is not an estimate of lost clicks.

**Risers and fallers** shows three queries per list, or up to five when expanded. The expand button appears only when there are more than three. If no query was observed in both periods, the card says that movement cannot be calculated instead of showing zero.

## Period and archive coverage

Choose 30, 90, 180, 480 or 1,825 days. The longest option covers the last five years of the archive, not all history. Month labels are approximate; the data details give exact dates on the America/Los_Angeles calendar. The period ends three days before today to allow for Google's reporting lag; the app does not verify completeness live. Imports request only data that Google marks as final.

The coverage details count days with a complete API response, days limited by the app, failed days and days of unknown coverage separately. Days already in the archive are not marked complete after the fact. Even a complete response lacks the queries Google hides for privacy. The last observed date and the date the archive was scanned through are different things.

## How the archive fills

While this screen is open, missing days load by themselves; **Search performance** also updates the archive while it is open. Nothing is fetched while both screens, or the app, are closed.

- After each limited transfer, the app waits 15 seconds before it requests the next chunk.
- Once the archive is current, it checks again every 15 minutes.
- After a connection or quota error, it waits 15 minutes before retrying.
- After an authorization error, you must renew the connection yourself.

**Continue filling archive** resumes the transfer by hand. The first import starts at the beginning of Google's 16-month retention window; days Google no longer serves cannot be recovered. Each run handles at most four time windows, and windows with many rows are split into days and continued in later runs. For one day the app reads up to the 50,000 rows Google serves; a day that still cannot be completed stays incomplete. The existing archive stays readable while it syncs.

## Position distribution

**Position distribution** covers every query observed in the current period. Positions are rounded, so 3.4 falls in the first band and 3.5 in the second. Bars are scaled to the largest band, and the percentage is each band's share of observed queries. Band changes are net changes across queries observed in both periods. A missing comparison is never shown as zero.

## Finding queries

Search and filters cover the entire archive. Filter counts take the search text and other active filters into account.

- **High impressions** includes queries tied at the upper-quartile threshold.
- **Period average in top 10** includes queries with no previous observation.
- **Dropped out of the top 10** requires an observation in both periods.

One button clears all filters. Pages hold 25, 50 or 100 queries; the summaries do not depend on page size.

Queries seen in the previous period but not in the current one have their own list, showing the first 25 by impressions and following the search text. Their absence does not prove a ranking loss or a position of zero.

## Reading a query's history

- Position averages are weighted by impressions.
- Change is the previous average minus the current average, so a positive number is an improvement.
- A change below 0.05 positions is shown as neutral; the significant-movement filters use 0.5.
- The detail uses the same periods as the table. The first and last recorded days are shown as separate evidence.

The number of observed days is always visible: 10 days out of a 90-day period is not full coverage. Daily points are spaced by real calendar dates, and gaps break the line. Whole missing weeks stay as gaps in weekly lines, and the first and last week can be partial. Use the arrow keys, Home and End to step through dates, or expand the daily values as a list.

The **Search performance** link keeps the exact query and dates. If the period is older than Google's 16-month window, the screen tells you the earliest date Google can still return before you leave.

Competitor rankings, search volume and traffic forecasts are not available.

---

# Opportunities

URL: https://seowatcher.io/en/docs/opportunities/

> Which page to work on first. Pages Google already shows, ranked by an upper bound on extra clicks from your own Search Console data.

**Opportunities** ranks the pages Google already shows for your site by how many extra clicks they could gain. The estimate uses your own Search Console data and your site's own click-through rates. Each page gets a suggested kind of work and an upper bound on the gain. It is not a forecast or a promise.

## Start here

The **Start here** card names the page with the largest estimated gain and the work to investigate first. It says nothing about how easy or quick that work is.

## Period and scope

Choose 7, 28 or 90 days. Search Console data covers complete days on Google's Pacific calendar; if Google does not report which days are final, the screen states the reporting lag it assumes. The exact start and end dates are always shown. Analytics reads the same calendar dates in the property's time zone, which can cover different hours.

Gains are shown per 30 days so that periods of different lengths compare. This is a scaled upper bound, not a calendar-month forecast or search volume. It counts only queries Google returned with enough data to estimate; the share of hidden queries is unknown, and row limits are stated. The current-click comparison uses all clicks on the candidate pages, brand clicks included.

The query estimate on the [Dashboard](https://seowatcher.io/en/docs/dashboard/) uses a different model and period. Do not add the two together.

## Four kinds of work

Each page falls into one kind of work, based on its measured queries:

| Kind of work                     | Situation                                                                           | Suggested action                           |
| -------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ |
| **Title and description work**   | On page one, but clicked less than your site's other searches at the same position. | **Rewrite the title and description**      |
| **On page one, positions 4-10**  | Below the top three. Moving up one band clearly raises clicks.                      | **Strengthen the content**                 |
| **On page two, positions 11-20** | Just behind page one; rarely clicked until it reaches page one.                     | **Add internal links, expand the content** |
| **Deep, beyond position 20**     | Has impressions, but a low position.                                                | **Review search intent and page coverage** |

## The worklist

Pages with an estimated gain come first, sorted by gain. Pages with impressions but no possible estimate follow, sorted by impressions. An unknown gain is not zero, and totals include only computed gains.

For a page with an unknown gain, the suggested work is based on position alone:

| Average position | Suggested work             |
| ---------------- | -------------------------- |
| 1–5              | Review title and snippet   |
| 6–10             | Improve content            |
| 11–20            | Internal links and content |
| 21 and below     | Check search intent        |

These suggestions do not prove a low CTR or a future gain. For a page with an unknown gain, look at the page and its observed queries first, and change the title or content only after you find a mismatch.

On a desktop the worklist is a sortable table; on a phone each page is a row with a **Details** action.

## Filters

Work filters follow the suggestions above. Conversion filters, such as **Show converting pages**, use observed Analytics data and appear only when matching pages exist. Work and conversion filters combine: a page must match both. The server filters every candidate page before showing the first 25, 50 or 100. Overall totals do not change with filters or row limits. A page can belong to several kinds of work, so their page counts do not add up. Period, row limit and filters are kept in the URL.

When every gain is unknown, the work categories show page counts without gain bars.

## Page details

**Details** shows each query's impressions, position, target position band and its share of the page's estimate. The top ten queries are listed, followed by the remainder; together they add up to the page's figure. Only non-brand queries are listed, and pages with only brand queries are marked. The CTR gap, in percentage points, compares like with like: comparable non-brand queries on the same impressions.

## Unknown and thin data

**Unestimable scope** counts pages that could not be estimated, broken down by reason: no matching queries, too few impressions or no target rate. These are separate from a measured zero. No page rows from Google does not prove the site had no impressions.

Thin data does not mean zero potential. Usable non-brand queries can be missing because Google hides them, because brand terms exclude them or because of row limits. Open **Search performance** to review the queries that do have impressions. The calculation details are under **Data coverage and calculation**.

## Analytics alongside

When GA4 is connected, each page shows observed organic sessions, key events and the share of sessions with a key event. The app never projects future conversions from extra clicks. Restricted metrics stay unknown, and source limits and time zones are named. URL variants can share one Analytics group, so do not add its sessions across rows. The conversion summary separates pages with a match from pages whose conversion status is unknown; missing Analytics data does not mean zero conversions, and the explanation appears in the page details rather than on every row.

**Inspect Analytics address group** on a row opens **Landing pages** in [Analytics](https://seowatcher.io/en/docs/analytics/) with the same dates and address group. When the address or dates cannot be matched, an explanation replaces the link. The group is filtered within the same source of up to 1,000 rows that Opportunities uses.

For a quota error, wait and refresh. For a permission error, check the project's connections. A failed refresh keeps the previous data with its original dates and a warning.

## Export and follow-up

**CSV** and **Export to Sheets** export the filtered rows with the observed dates, the 30-day unit, the model, property, brand source, source limits and Analytics group. Unknown gains are blank, and each row carries its status, reason, brand marker and observed queries. Nothing is written to Sheets until you select the export.

**Open in Search performance** opens the page's detail panel for the same dates. If those dates cannot be read, the screen says so instead of switching to other dates.

After you change a page, note the date, then compare measured clicks, CTR and position over equivalent periods. A smaller estimate on its own does not prove success. A low position or a low estimate is no reason to delete content; merge pages only after confirming that they serve the same intent.

---

# Saved keywords

URL: https://seowatcher.io/en/docs/saved-keywords/

> Follow the queries you care about with dated Search Console observations from the local archive, and see which ones moved.

**Saved keywords** is your shortlist of queries. You add them from **Search performance** or **Rank tracking** with **Save as keyword**. Saving does not start a separate tracker at Google: the screen matches your list against Search Console observations already stored in the local archive, which **Rank tracking** fills.

## Period and dates

Choose 30, 90 or 180 days; the default is 90. The screen shows the exact dates of the current period and of the previous period of equal length. Dates follow Google's Pacific calendar and assume a three-day reporting lag. That assumption does not prove the archive is complete for those dates.

## Summary cards

The cards count the saved keywords that match your text and tag filters: how many were observed, how many moved significantly between the two periods, and how many have no position data (**Position unknown**). The band bars use the same set; select a band to narrow the table. These counts cover your saved keywords only, not every query of the site, and they are not search volume.

When no keyword can be compared, the movement card says **No comparison** instead of zero. When every saved keyword was observed, the **Position unknown** card shows no warning. A card's button is disabled when it has no matching keywords.

## How keywords are matched and measured

- Matching ignores extra spaces and follows Turkish case rules, so `I`/`ı` and `İ`/`i` are treated as different letters.
- All raw query variants that match a keyword are combined, weighted by impressions.
- Position is the impression-weighted average.
- A significant movement is a change of at least half a position. Smaller changes are visible in the row's details.
- A keyword without observations is never shown as position zero or as a proven loss. "No comparison" is different from "No change".

Keywords saved for a specific market keep their own record and counts, but archive observations always cover all countries and devices.

## The table

The table shows the keyword, average position, change, impressions and tags. On a phone the key figures sit under the keyword. You can sort by date added (the default), position, change, impressions or keyword. **Review declines** sorts the significant declines first so you can investigate them; it does not explain their cause.

**Archive details** on a row shows the same dates, the matched raw variants, the previous average, the number of observed days and the saved market. The date the keyword was added and any intent recorded by older versions also appear there; intent is not measured again. **Show daily archive observations** loads the daily history for the same dates on request. Missing days stay as gaps, the dates can be inspected with the keyboard, and a text list of the values is included.

The **Search performance** link on a row searches for the keyword text in that screen's live last-28-day view. It is a quick look, not an exact match of the archive figures.

## Filters, selection and bulk actions

- Include terms must all match; exclude terms must all be absent. Each box takes up to 20 terms.
- Selecting several tags shows keywords that have any of them, up to 50 selected tags. Tag counts are project-wide.
- Filters, band, period, sort order and page are stored in the URL. **Clear all** also clears an active band that has no results.

A selection covers the current page only. While a filter or refresh is pending, actions on the old rows are disabled. Removing keywords asks for confirmation. Editing or deleting a tag never deletes keywords.

## Exports

**Download CSV** and **Export to Sheets** export the filtered keywords. The keyword, intent, tags and date added come first. The remaining columns are current and previous position, change, status, observed days, exact dates, coverage, variants, scope, market, record ID and snapshot. Unknown values are left blank. If the data changes during an export, start the export again.

## When data is missing

The screen explains each case separately: Search Console not connected, archive never imported, archive incomplete for the period, or a failed read. **Refresh list** only re-reads the local database. To fetch newer data from Google, update the archive on **Rank tracking**, after connecting Search Console if needed. Google omits rare queries, so a keyword missing from the archive may still appear in search.

---

# Understanding Analytics data

URL: https://seowatcher.io/en/docs/analytics/

> Read GA4 sessions, engagement, key events and revenue for your site, check the measurement setup and export the rows you need.

The **Analytics** screen reads the GA4 property connected to the project. An overview of sessions, engagement rate, key events and purchase revenue sits at the top. Below it, the report selector offers **Landing pages**, **Pages and screens**, **Traffic acquisition**, **Key events**, **Ecommerce**, **Site search**, **Audience** and **Measurement health**. Notes on how to read the numbers are collapsed under **Understanding Analytics data**; the scope, dates and warnings always stay visible.

## Scope: channel, property and dates

**Organic Search** is the default channel. It includes every search engine, not only Google. **All traffic** switches both the overview and the report. **Site search** always covers all traffic and has no channel switch.

The figures cover every host and data stream in the property. If another site or app sends data to the same property, it is included.

**Last 7 days**, **Last 28 days** and **Last 3 months** (90 days) end yesterday in the property's time zone. The screen shows the current dates, the previous period of equal length and the time zone. Yesterday is a completed calendar day, but GA4 may still reprocess recent days. A link can set exact `startDate` and `endDate` values; an end date in the future is moved back to yesterday with a notice.

GA4 and Search Console use different calendars (property time zone versus Pacific time) and different measures. The same date labels can cover different hours.

## Reading the overview

- **Key events** count events, not unique customers.
- **Engagement duration** is total time, not an average per user.
- **Revenue** of zero does not prove the site has no shop. An unknown currency is named next to the amount.
- Daily values separate an unknown day from a day with zero.
